While some Wall Street pros caution that the historical cyclicality of memory demand makes those low multiples contrarian warning signals, the size and scale of the AI buildout could render comparisons to previous cycles irrelevant. Analysts’ price target for Seagate indicates the shares will rise more than 70% over the next 12 months, while Sandisk is expected to climb more than 80%. Of the 74 stocks in the S&P information technology sector, Micron, Seagate, Sandisk and Western Digital are among the top seven in return potential, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

“People rightfully get nervous when you see a selloff, because you don’t know if it’s the top or just some air coming out before another cycle higher,” Bakhos said. “Profit takers are winning the battle now, but I think the long-term holders are in a strong position.”

title: Mi Material's IPO 2.2 times subscribed
article:
The IPO of Mi Material, which raised a total of $294 million at $1.80 each, was 2.1 times subscribed.

The public offer of slightly over 6.2 million shares was just 1.3 times taken, while the international offer of nearly 71.3 million shares was 2.2 times subscribed.

Another 41.9 million shares have been sold to seven cornerstone investors: abrdn Asia, abrdn Malaysia, Amova Asset Management Asia, Areca Capital, Barings Singapore, Fullerton Fund Management and Manulife Investment Management (Singapore).

Amova and Fullerton, both of which are among the EQDP fund managers, took up more shares as part of the international offer as well.

AR Capital, another EQDP fund manager, took part in the international offer too.

Trading will start at 2 pm on Oct 28.

See also: Dubai firm’s US$543 mil IPO covered within minutes despite war

Mi Material, which is spun off from Bursa-listed Mi Technovation, plays in the semiconductor manufacturing chain by supplying materials used in the packaging of chips.

CEO Kevin Tan Kiang Hiong says he is "encouraged" by the support shown by investors.

For its most recent 1HFY2026, Mi Material recorded earnings of US$14.3 million, up from US$2.9 million in the year earlier. Revenue in the same period more than doubled to US$53.7 million.

See also: Anthropic flags ‘existential risks’ in long-awaited IPO filing

As indicated in its prospectus, Mi Material expects to report further growth in the 3QFY2026 ended Sept 30.

Revenue is seen to jump 15.6% to US$37.8 million and with gross profit margin seen to hold steady versus 2QFY2026, Mi Material expects higher profit before tax versus the preceding quarter.

The company will report its 3QFY2026 in a business update after market on Oct 29.

title: Intel said to buy quantum start-up Classiq for about US$2.3 bil
article:
(Oct 27): Intel Corp agreed to buy Israeli start-up Classiq Technologies Ltd as part of a push to capitalise on quantum computing, a still-nascent field that is seeking commercial applications.

The chipmaker will pay about US$2.3 billion ($2.9 billion) for Classiq, according to people familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified because the information is private. Intel announced the deal ahead of its third-quarter earnings report on Thursday, but did not disclose a price. Israeli newspaper Calcalist reported the value previously.

Intel, once the world’s largest chipmaker, wants to ensure that it doesn’t miss out on quantum technology, a potentially large new market for the semiconductor industry. Chief executive officer Lip-Bu Tan is seeking to regain ground lost to rivals in artificial intelligence (AI) computing.

“Joining forces with Classiq transforms Intel’s Quantum Computing Group into a full-stack quantum computing business,” Tan said in a statement. The companies expect the transaction to close in the first half of 2027.

Classiq offers its customers, which include BMW AG and AT&T Inc, access to specially developed AI tools that help them test out the usefulness of quantum for their operations. The company, which has raised more than US$200 million in funding and has about 130 employees, will continue to help clients develop code that runs on multiple types of quantum hardware — even if it is sourced from Intel’s competitors.

Quantum computing relies on the manipulation of subatomic particles to speed up data crunching. Though still a fledgling industry, the field has gained interest from large technology companies seeking an edge over traditional computer processing. But the massive complexity of quantum hardware makes it difficult to deploy at a large scale.

See also: EQT to buy Range Resources, creating largest US gas producer

Intel has been working to parlay its strengths in silicon-based component manufacturing into a role in quantum computing for more than a decade. Like others, it sees quantum components working alongside traditional computers, not replacing them wholesale. It’s focused on a technology called spin qubits.

“This revolution is about the shift from science to engineering,” said Classiq CEO Nir Minerbi, who co-founded the start-up in 2020. “When you think engineering, you think Intel.”

title: Instagram ramps up video strategy in escalating TikTok, YouTube rivalry
article:
(Oct 27): Meta Platforms Inc's Instagram is pushing deeper into video with new products to help it compete more aggressively with TikTok and Google’s YouTube, and lay the foundation for its big swing in television.

The new products include Features, which are horizontal videos of as long as 90 minutes, and Series, designed for episodic, short-form microdramas. The company is also rebooting Instagram Live, which has been around for a decade, to make the streaming feature more ubiquitous and discoverable across the app, even to non-followers, in the Reels tab.

“Our goal is really to be the best place for social entertainment,” said Tessa Lyons, Instagram’s vice-president of product overseeing the video expansion under Instagram chief Adam Mosseri. “To do that well, we need to broaden the way that we enable people to tell stories through video and enable audiences to discover them.” A huge part of that is TV, she added, where people are spending more time streaming videos — especially creator-led content.

The shift comes as Instagram is seeing all-time highs in engagement driven mainly by video, Meta chief executive officer Mark Zuckerberg said when the company reported third-quarter earnings last week. At the same time, the platform, which first rose to prominence as a photo-sharing app, faces intensifying competition with TikTok and YouTube and has been somewhat slower in developing a more entertainment-focused strategy.

TikTok has already helped popularise microdramas, short-form soap operas for smartphones that took off in China and are gaining traction across the West, while YouTube recently introduced “Shorts series” to help creators organise their work into episodes and seasons. YouTube has been investing for close to a decade in its "living room" strategy aimed at getting YouTube videos onto every screen in the home, making the video giant all but synonymous with modern-day TV.

Lyons acknowledged “we are in a very competitive market” but said Instagram has a unique advantage because it was built more on social connections and the premise of sharing with friends, a key value-add for creators eager to grow and nurture relationships with their fanbases.

See also: Memory stocks lost their shine despite strong earnings

“Creators don't just want to put content out in the world,” she said. “They want to feel like they are building a community around that content that's deeply engaged with them.”

The success of Instagram Reels has also set up the platform to excel in other video formats, Lyons added, noting that people reshare those short, vertical video clips in direct messages 4.5 billion times a day.

But Reels has a key limitation: Those over three minutes long are not recommended to new audiences, so comedians, podcasters, video bloggers and others have had to drive viewers off Instagram to keep them watching and engaging with content. Features are aimed at solving that problem by keeping users on-platform and enabling creators to experiment more freely with the length of their videos on both mobile and TV. Beginning Monday, a beta version will be available to tens of thousands of creators in the US.

See also: Applied Materials ups stake in BE Semiconductor to about 20%

Series, the medium tailored to booming short-form dramas, is in testing with a smaller subset of creators in the US, Mexico and India. Instagram’s surfacing of livestreams in recommendations and Reels is also in testing, set to launch in Indonesia and Brazil by year end. Within the app, all of these formats will eventually be shown alongside Reels.

Instagram has been pursuing TV as a big swing in the US since last year, when it unveiled its first dedicated TV app allowing users to watch Reels on a larger screen. Since beginning as a test on Amazon.com Inc’s Fire TV platform in December, those efforts have expanded to Samsung and Google TV. Instagram for TV launches on Monday on Apple TV in the US, eventually moving beyond Reels alone to include the newly announced video formats, and soon, viewers will also be able to use their phones as remotes. Still, Lyons cautioned, “the TV bet is really early” and will be a multi-year journey.

“We are not at a stage right now where we are trying to grow the TV bet — we are really trying to figure out what's working for audiences on TV — but we do think that that's going to be a key part of the next few years of Instagram,” including outside the US in the near future, she said.

“If behaviour [and] the consumption of these platforms is moving to TV,” Mosseri said last year in an interview with Bloomberg, “then we need to move to TV, too.”

title: US orders for durable goods increase by most in five months
article:
(Oct 27): US orders for durable goods rose in September by the most in five months, on stronger bookings for aircraft and other business equipment, adding to evidence of momentum in manufacturing.

The value of orders for durable goods, meant to last at least three years, increased 1.8% after an upwardly revised 0.1% gain in the prior month, Commerce Department figures showed on Tuesday.

Core capital goods orders, a proxy for investment in equipment that excludes the volatile aircraft and military hardware categories, increased 0.5% last month.

The durables report showed a 28.4% increase in commercial aircraft orders. Boeing Co reported more orders in September compared with the prior month. Bookings for computers, machinery and motor vehicles also rose.

Business investment has been robust this year, led by spending related to artificial intelligence. The durables report suggests that trend continued through September, setting the stage for a strong capital spending reading when the government issues its initial estimate of third-quarter (3Q) gross domestic product on Thursday.

Non-defence capital goods shipments including aircraft, which feed into the equipment investment portion of the GDP report, rose 1.7%. The government uses data on shipments as an input to GDP rather than orders, which can be canceled.

See also: US consumer sentiment slips to five-month low on inflation

Before the report, the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta’s GDPNow forecast anticipated business spending on equipment would add one percentage point to 3Q growth.

Core capital goods shipments, a less volatile metric that excludes planes and military hardware, rose 1.2% — extending a stretch of robust advances.

Economists prefer the core equipment shipments figure to gauge underlying capital investment since there are extremely long times between ordering aircraft and military hardware and the actual shipment taking place.

title: Acts of God meet acts of AI in private equity’s new debt play
article:
(Oct 27): Force majeure has long protected companies from acts of God. Now some borrowers want protection from acts of AI.

Private equity firms are adding force majeure-style clauses to new buyouts that could let companies stop the clock on addressing defaults they determine were caused by AI disruption.

HIG Capital managed to get the language included in the €470 million loan backing its majority stake in Terras Group, a German-headquartered provider of infrastructure engineering and construction services, according to people familiar with the deal who did not want to be identified discussing private details.

Years of strong demand have allowed private equity firms to chip away at lender protections. But several creditors said the new language goes further than usual and has appeared in at least two leveraged buyout financings since September.

“Lenders and investors are closely reviewing language proposed by sponsors that seeks to permit event of default flexibility in connection with AI,” said Jeremy Duffy, a partner and chair of European leveraged finance at Cahill Gordon & Reindel LLP. “It’s a fast-moving piece of the leveraged finance documentation pie.”

Artificial intelligence is threatening to upend every business model and the debt structures built around them. Buyout firms are particularly exposed after amassing a big bet on software-as-a-service firms, now vulnerable to AI disruption.

See also: Meta upsizes equity offering as it seeks almost US$98 bil

A force majeure clause is typically invoked by companies to waive contractual obligations in a catastrophe — usually reserved for so-called acts of God like hurricanes and earthquakes, the Covid-19 pandemic or the 9/11 terror attacks.

In this case, HIG Capital is adapting force majeure language to stop the clock on a default if Terras Group is disrupted by the impact of AI or an array of other situations. These include Covid-19 or any other pandemic, a substantial increase of energy or resource pricing, war and terrorism, according to people familiar with the documentation.

See also: OCBC draws AI ideas from staff beyond tech teams as it builds skills across the bank

Some creditors argue that the proposed provisions undermine a basic premise of lending: even when things go wrong, you still expect to get your money back.

When companies miss an interest payment, they are usually allowed a grace period, typically 30 days, to make the payment before a default is called. After that, lenders can demand their money back.

Officially, the new provisions seek to extend grace periods. But in practice, AI disruption, unlike a pandemic, has no clear end date.

HIG’s clause would allow Terras to defer the consequences of not paying back interest for as long as it feels the impact of AI, said a person familiar with the deal. The company still owes interest but lenders’ remedies are suspended.

Lenders succeeded in having similar language struck from Bain Capital’s €4.7 billion-equivalent leveraged-loan deal for its acquisition of a controlling stake in Volkswagen AG’s heavy diesel-engine unit Everllence, said the people.

The market’s approach to investor protections has become increasingly split. Private equity sponsors are being aggressive in cases where the credit deals they expect will perform well but are re-inserting covenants to deals in troubled sectors like software.

HIG Capital was advised by a group of partners from law firm Paul, Weiss including Neel Sachdev, a powerful private equity lawyer who has played a big part in encouraging buyout firms to slash creditor protections in financing.

Representatives at HIG and Bain declined to comment while Sachdev didn’t reply to a request for comment.

title: Singapore’s EMA backs grid resilience projects with $14.9 mil
article:
Singapore’s Energy Market Authority (EMA) has awarded $14.9 million to four projects aimed at keeping its electricity grid reliable as more solar panels and electric vehicle chargers connect to it.

The work comes as Singapore plans for higher power demand. In a five-year infrastructure plan announced yesterday, EMA says peak demand could rise from 8.6 gigawatts in August to as much as 13 gigawatts by 2031.

EMA awarded $8.7 million to two projects by SP PowerAssets under the SP Technology Laboratory, which EMA and SP Group established to develop ways to prepare the grid for future needs.

One project will use AI and data to guide maintenance and renewal decisions for grid infrastructure. The other will test ways to manage voltage and power quality as more solar panels and electric vehicle chargers connect to the grid.

Meanwhile, Yokogawa Engineering Asia received $4.2 million to develop support that can respond quickly when the power system is disturbed. Its project will examine whether batteries, solar inverters, industrial electricity users and EVs can be coordinated to provide that support.

The remaining $2 million went to Green Union. It will develop ways to coordinate solar panels, battery storage systems and EVs so they can contribute to grid operations and make better use of existing infrastructure. The project is funded under a joint grant by EMA and the Korean Institute of Energy Technology Evaluation and Planning (KETEP), which supports industry-led research into using such resources to strengthen the power system.

See also: Sembcorp and ST Engineering prepare for nuclear future

Separately, EMA has helped update guidance on how companies substantiate claims that they use renewable electricity in Singapore. Enterprise Singapore, through the Singapore Standards Council, revised Singapore Standard 673 with EMA and the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry.

Under the revised standard, companies making such claims should use renewable energy certificates tied to electricity supplied to Singapore’s grid. This includes certificates from domestic renewable generation and approved electricity imports connected to the grid.

See also: Singapore shields itself from energy risks as Indonesia cuts gas

Companies can still buy certificates from overseas renewable projects that do not supply electricity to Singapore to support renewable energy development.

The standard says they should not use those certificates for market-based Scope 2 claims about electricity consumed here. Scope 2 covers emissions associated with electricity a company purchases.

title: Applied Materials ups stake in BE Semiconductor to about 20%
article:
(Oct 27): Applied Materials Inc boosted its stake in fellow chip-equipment maker BE Semiconductor Industries NV and said it plans to work more closely with the European company, which is becoming a more important part of the artificial intelligence (AI) computing supply chain.

Applied’s stake will increase to about 20% of outstanding shares, the US company said in a statement on Monday. The company first disclosed a 9% stake in BE Semiconductor, known as Besi, last year.

Besi shares rose as much as 10% in Amsterdam trading on Tuesday, the biggest intraday gain since March. The stock has gained 19% this year, giving it a market value of about €12.9 billion. Applied closed 2.7% higher at US$387.59 in New York on Monday.

Companies that make equipment for AI and the data centres that run the technology are seeing surging demand. Besi specialises in hybrid bonding, a technology used in chip assembly that boosts AI performance. Last week, the company rebuffed analysts’ concerns that larger chip-equipment maker ASML Holding NV was emerging as a competitor.

Applied’s investment follows a six-year collaboration between the two companies. Besi also recently joined Applied’s new chip-equipment research facility known as the EPIC Center.

Though Applied described its investment as “long term”, the company said a bigger takeover is not in the works. “Applied currently has no intention to increase its investment in Besi beyond approximately 20%, and Applied does not intend to seek board representation at Besi,” the company said.

See also: Apple’s foldable iPhone Duo draws early complaints of the screen cracking

title: Coca-Cola raises guidance, buoyed by soda sales abroad
article:
(Oct 27): Coca-Cola Co raised its 2026 full-year outlook on strong international demand for soda, especially its zero-sugar drinks.

The beverage company now sees organic sales increasing at least 5% this year, rather than growing about that much. Coca-Cola had already raised its guidance in July, pointing to the company’s increasing confidence in the year’s results.

“Our results this quarter demonstrate our system’s sustained momentum, giving us confidence in our updated full-year guidance,” CEO Henrique Braun said in a statement.

The Atlanta-based company said it saw 5% growth in unit case volume sales of sparkling soft drinks, including 16% growth of Coca-Cola Zero Sugar and 6% growth of Diet Coke. However, in North America, growth in Coca-Cola soda was offset by a decline in water, sports, coffee and tea. Sales volume in North America was flat, coming in below the average of analysts’ estimates of 2.3% growth.

Shares of Coca-Cola were little changed at 7.28am in premarket New York trading. The stock has gained almost 33% this year through Monday’s close, compared with a 12% increase in the S&P 500 Index. PepsiCo stock has declined 6% over the same period.

Coca-Cola’s third-quarter adjusted earnings per share were 91 cents, topping the average of analyst estimates compiled by Bloomberg. Organic sales, which strip out items such as currency volatility, rose 7%, above expectations.

See also: Starbucks says it’s not buying Chipotle, dousing deal rumours

Coca-Cola’s widening portfolio of beverages is reaching more shoppers, with zero-sugar soda, higher-protein Fairlife milk and water as many consumers turn away from traditional full-calorie soft drinks. Coca-Cola has also nabbed some recent wins against rival PepsiCo Inc, including taking over KFC’s US restaurants.

title: ST Engineering won $5.6 bil worth of new contracts in 3QFY2026
article:
Singapore Technologies Engineering has won contracts worth some $5.6 billion in 3QFY2026, bringing the nine-month total to $13.2 billion.

The strong third quarter was driven by broad-base wins across all three business segments, with commercial aerospace securing $1.4 billion, defence & public security $1.8 billion and urban solutions & satcom $2.4 billion.

According to ST Engineering, contracts won by USS include those for major train works in Taiwan and also Singapore.

Its electronic road tolling business also won contracts to advance Dubai's tolling system, modernise tolling infrastructure for the Tampa-Hillsborough Expressway Authority, and deliver back-office solutions and RFID tags in the US as well.

Also, in Singapore, the company won contracts to provide integrated smart security management solutions for public and private sector customers.

The Satcom business secured various contracts for the deployments of its multi-orbit ‘Intuition’ platform including one with Datacom and expanded mission-critical government and defence networks. It also supported satellite operator modernisation programmes across Europe, Africa, the Middle East and Asia.

See also: Yangzijiang Maritime to sell six vessels for US$308 million

For the company's commercial aerospace segment, new contracts won include its first Airbus A220 airframe heavy maintenance contract with an Asia-Pacific operator, expanding its support capabilities for next-generation narrowbody platforms beyond the Airbus A320neo and Boeing 737 MAX.

It also secured airframe maintenance agreements with Asia Pacific airline customers, an exclusive two-year CFM56-7B engines Performance Restoration Shop Visit services agreement with Hebei Airlines and a multi-year component MRO agreement with Collins Aerospace.

As for its DPS segment, it won a five-year contract to supply 40mm ammunition to the UK Ministry of Defence, alongside additional ammunition orders from international customers.

See also: Soilbuild Construction wins $103 mil worth of new contracts

The digital systems under DPS also won projects for its data centre services, public safety digital infrastructure and defence command-and-control systems. A satellite ground station and maintenance programme was also secured in Sweden.

In cybersecurity, it secured contracts for new products, services and solutions from defence and commercial customers in Singapore.

Its Marine and Defence Aerospace businesses in Singapore expanded MRO support for the United States Naval Ship fleet and international C-130 operators.

ST Engineering shares closed at $10.16 on Oct 27, down 0.2%.

title: Universal Music discussed going private with buyout firms
article:
(Oct 27): Universal Music Group, the world’s largest record company, has discussed going private with a few prominent Wall Street firms, according to people familiar with the matter.

Universal’s management held preliminary conversations with private equity firms including Apollo Global Management Inc, TPG Inc and Blackstone Inc earlier this year, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the talks were confidential. The board of the company, with a market value of €29 billion (RM132.74 billion), is aware of the discussions, they added.

The conversations have not progressed nor has Universal, home to acts including Taylor Swift, The Weeknd and Kendrick Lamar, begun a sales process, the people said.

The company declined to comment, as did the private equity firms. Universal’s sagging share price has prompted many at the company and on Wall Street to wonder whether the music giant would be better off as a private firm.

Shares in Universal rose as much as 6% in Amsterdam trading on Tuesday, the biggest intraday gain since April. The stock has declined about 27% this year and trades below the price at which the company first went public in 2021. Catalogues and other music assets are trading at much higher multiples than Universal and rival Warner Music Group on the private market.

Universal, led by CEO Lucian Grainge, was already the target of one takeover attempt this year when shareholder Bill Ackman made an offer to buy the Amsterdam-listed company and move its listing to the US. Universal rejected the bid but the company’s largest shareholder agreed with Ackman that the firm is undervalued. Universal is the largest and most successful of the three major record label groups, the distributor of nine of the 10 best-selling acts in the world last year. Sony Group Corp is another major competitor.

See also: Orange boosts profit outlook after Africa, Middle East growth

“We think that the price is not right at all,” Cyrille Bollore, whose family owns a 30% stake in Universal Music Group, said at his firm’s shareholder meeting in May. Bollore praised Universal as one of his family’s best investments and a hedge against an economic downturn. “Perhaps we’ll sell a few per cent one day. We’ll see. But we can’t sell too early.”

Any deal would require the assent of the Bollore family, which owns more than 30% of the firm between the personal holdings of Vincent Bollore, Cyrille’s father, and Vivendi, their media company. Vivendi used to own Universal Music before the company was spun out as a separate public company.

The Bollores haven’t signalled interest in selling their full position. Nor has Chinese internet giant Tencent Holdings Ltd, which owns more than 11%. Taking Universal public was lucrative for the Bollores and a handful of senior leaders who had stock. The company has since struggled to satisfy investors.

See also: Japan vows to address cyber attack on FX with urgency

Record labels have surrendered market share to independent distributors offering more artist-friendly terms. The streaming market that boosted sales for the last decade has slowed in the US and Western Europe over the last couple of years. The fastest-growing markets are in Latin America and Asia, regions where the major record labels are less dominant.

The biggest drag on the stock of Universal and Warner Music has been anxiety about artificial intelligence. AI has produced a surge in the number of songs getting uploaded to streaming services, which analysts and investors fear will dilute the labels’ share of listening and earnings.

Grainge has said Universal isn’t at risk of dilution. “We anticipated the rise of AI slop and we anticipated the potential for fraud,” Grainge said on a call with analysts in July. “Music platforms should reward creativity and guard against illegally trained AI models pumping AI slop or fraud designed to divert royalties from artists, songwriters, labels and music publishers.”

Universal has expressed concern about AI companies violating its copyrights, as file-sharing websites did during the internet boom. Universal sued Suno, the largest AI music company, as well as Anthropic.

title: Aramco contains fire near Ras Tanura oil hub after attack — Bloomberg
article:
(Oct 27): Saudi Arabia contained a fire near its biggest oil export terminal at Ras Tanura on the Persian Gulf following an attack in the region, a person with knowledge of the matter said.

The blaze occurred during the early hours of Tuesday near facilities operated by state producer Saudi Aramco, the person said, asking not to be identified because the matter is private. The extent of the damage wasn’t immediately clear.

The company’s press office and the kingdom’s Energy Ministry didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure has come under repeated attacks from Yemen’s Houthi militants in recent weeks, with Aramco’s headquarters, a major oil field and refineries in the kingdom’s western region targeted. Ras Tanura, located in the east, hosts crucial facilities for loading oil tankers, plus the kingdom’s biggest refinery and a swathe of storage tanks.

Saudi Arabia said on Tuesday that air defences intercepted and destroyed three ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards the kingdom’s eastern region.

See also: Oil declines as Iran diplomacy picks up before Israeli, US votes

Oil reversed earlier losses, with Brent crude trading near US$116 a barrel in London. Prices have jumped about 13% so far this month as traders weigh the potential for a resumption of fighting between the US and Iran.

Both sides have held off major military operations in recent weeks, while Saudi Arabia has suffered attacks from Iran-backed groups like the Houthis in Yemen and militias in Iraq.

When the conflict began in February, Aramco began sending the bulk of its exports from its Red Sea coast after Iran blocked much of the traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. In recent weeks, the company has been stepping up crude exports from the Persian Gulf again.

See also: Woodside sells stake in long-stalled Timor-Leste LNG project

That’s partly because tanker operators have been finding ways to restore shipping flows through Hormuz, with traffic reaching almost prewar levels. It also reflects growing Houthi threats to shipping and ports in the Red Sea.

title: CGAC, SGX RegCo’s proposed changes to corporate governance code and listing rules include cap on directorships
article:
The Corporate Governance Advisory Committee (CGAC) and the Singapore Exchange Regulation (SGX RegCo) are proposing several changes to the Code of Corporate Governance (Code) and SGX Listing Rules. The changes are meant to complement with the Equities Market Review Group’s earlier announced initiatives while helping to strengthen corporate governance and sustain investor confidence, says CGAC and SGX RegCo in a statement on Oct 27.

CGAC and SGX RegCo have launched a public consultation to obtain feedback on the proposed changes. The consultation will run from Oct 27, 2026 to Jan 27, 2027. CGAC and SGX RegCo’s proposed changes fall under three broad areas: facilitating effective implementation of the Code, enhancing board independence and quality as well as sharpening the focus on value creation.

“We are not trying to create rigid, restrictive rules about what companies disclose and how they disclose it. We are trying to create a structure and framework that helps every enterprise reach its growth objectives,” SGX RegCo CEO Tan Boon Gin says of the proposed changes.

Under the first area, CGAC and SGX RegCo are proposing that the Code and Practice Guidance be updated to reflect intended outcomes and illustrative examples. This will help to provide greater clarity on how the Code’s principles can be achieved.

Code provisions apply to listed companies on a comply-or-explain basis while the provisions under the Practice Guidance are purely voluntary. Compliance with SGX Listing Rules is mandatory for all listed companies.

The changes under the second area aim to make boards more effective by ensuring strong governance arrangements and the appointment of high-quality directors. To that end, CGAC and SGX RegCo are proposing a new Code provision for companies where the CEO is concurrently serving as the board chair to explain how the chair’s role is effectively fulfilled and to disclose the safeguards in place. Companies will be required under the SGX Listing Rules to appoint a lead independent director when the chair is not independent.

See also: Seven Singapore-listed names among ‘global sector leaders’ in annual real estate ESG benchmark

Other proposed changes to the SGX Listing Rules include requiring key board committees, including the nominating committee, remuneration committee and audit committee to be chaired by an independent director and comprise a majority of independent directors.

Companies will also be required to disclose, explicitly, the selection criteria and considerations for board appointments as well as whether board members have undergone professional development activities relevant to their roles. In addition, CGAC and SGX RegCo are proposing a cap on the number to listed-entity directorships an individual can hold at any time to no more than five.

As for the third and final area, CGAC and SGX RegCo are proposing refinements to Code provisions to reinforce the responsibility of boards to oversee strategy, long-term value creation and investor engagement. Additionally, companies will be required to disclose their capital management policies.

See also: SIAS CEO welcomes rising corporate governance standards but notes gap between large and small companies

Earlier, on Sept 23, SGX RegCo introduced new rules requiring companies to disclose their dividend policy to shareholders. The changes, which apply to annual reports for financial years commencing on or after Jan 1, 2027, do not require issuers to commit to a dividend payout.

“A boilerplate disclosure is better than no disclosure at all,” Tan says. “In a disclosure-based regime, a baseline disclosure forms an essential starting point for investor assessment and engagement. It gives the market a benchmark. Investors can compare issuers: The one with a detailed capital management policy will naturally capture more trust and a premium. The one with a boilerplate will be left behind.”

CGAC says it will consider the feedback received before making its final recommendations to the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and SGX on the Code and SGX Listing Rules respectively. Thereafter, MAS and SGX will consider CGAC’s recommendations before deciding on the final amendments, implementation timelines and transitional arrangements.

title: Pop Mart's 3Q sales fall up to 50% as Labubu fad cools
article:
(Oct 27): Pop Mart International Group Ltd reported a decline in third-quarter (3Q) sales from a year earlier, hurt by fading Labubu momentum and a tough base of comparison following last year’s blockbuster results.

Overall revenue fell as much as 50% from a year ago in the three months ended September, according to Pop Mart’s latest business update based on preliminary data. That compares with revenue growth of about 250% in the year-ago period. Revenue in China declined 25% to 30%, while sales from the Americas fell 70% to 75%.

The downturn underscores the volatility that can accompany an unexpected viral hit. Demand for Labubu — the snaggle-toothed monster plush — reached fever pitch in 2025 with everyone from K-pop idols to Hollywood celebrities and ordinary consumers seeking one. The results also highlight mounting pressure on the company as investors grapple with softening demand this year in its home market alongside persistent weakness across overseas operations.

While Pop Mart has described 2026 as “a year of adjustment”, investors are concerned that the slowdown could extend into 2027. HSBC Holdings plc cut its revenue forecasts for 2027 and 2028 by 8% and 9%, respectively, in a research note released ahead of the results, citing expectations for “a longer road to stabilisation”. The bank also lowered its 2026 sales estimate to 33.2 billion yuan from 34.6 billion yuan previously.

In a bid to maximise brand exposure and keep consumer buzz alive, Pop Mart continued expanding its retail footprint through flagship locations in key domestic and international markets. The company opened a three-story flagship store near West Lake in Hangzhou and launched its European flagship on Boulevard Haussmann in Paris in September. It also rolled out new releases tied to popular intellectual properties, including Twinkle Twinkle and Dimoo, during 3Q.

title: French consumer confidence drops to 13-year low following riots
article:
(Oct 27): French consumer confidence plummeted to its lowest level in 13 years in October as households reckoned with multiple shocks from a bond market selloff to protests that descended into rioting.

The monthly gauge dropped five points to 80 with respondents becoming more concerned about their financial situation, living standards and unemployment, statistics agency Insee said on Tuesday. That’s below the median estimate of 85 in a Bloomberg survey and lower than any economist forecast.

 

The reading has been stuck below its long-term average of 100 for five years amid bouts of inflation and political and budget instability.

But the backdrop has worsened significantly in recent weeks with the minority government entering another showdown over austerity measures, a surge in borrowing costs as investors dump French bonds and an escalation of student protests.

The tensions boiled over on Oct 17 with violence breaking out around cost-of-living demonstrations, looting across the country and thousands of arrests.

Insee’s latest consumer confidence measure doesn’t reflect the full impact of the upheaval: while the the cutoff was Oct 19, most of the responses are collected at the start of the three-week survey period.

See also: Germany’s business outlook in October unexpectedly improves for sixth month

“Weak sentiment is likely to weigh on spending as political uncertainty increases. This brings further downside risks to our fourth-quarter growth forecast,” says Jean Dalbard, economist at Bloomberg Economics.

In an attempt to calm the unrest that began with students blocking high schools, the French government announced on Monday it will overhaul the system for allocating university places, limit some class sizes and provide loans for building renovations.

See also: EU plans to hit China with more import curbs in early 2027 — Bloomberg

But protests are set to continue on Saturdays as well as a day of demonstrations and strikes on Nov 5 that’s backed by the country’s biggest trade unions.

President Emmanuel Macron said on Monday he would also maintain a heightened security presence, similar to the deployment that ensured relative calm on Saturday.

“It’s not normal that six months before a presidential election, our country should be in such a state of turmoil,” he said after visiting police in Marseille. “Some people are happy to see disorder, I’m not — never again another Oct 17.”

Details of Insee’s survey showed that assessments of past living standards dropped to the lowest since the agency began measuring in 1972. Meanwhile, unemployment expectations rose to the highest since the Covid pandemic and consumers’ outlook for their financial situation was the gloomiest in four years.

The report also showed heightened inflation expectations as the proportion of households who foresee price increases in the next twelve months advanced.

Data on Friday is expected to show inflation accelerated further to 3.6% this month. A reading of gross domestic product, also due that day, will likely reveal that the economy expanded only 0.1% in the third quarter after stagnating in the previous three months and contracting at the start of the year.

title: STTGDC gets US$590 mil green loan for Tokyo data centre fit-out
article:
ST Telemedia Global Data Centres (STTGDC) has secured a US$590 million ($756 million) green loan to fit out and operate two data centres near Tokyo, giving it funding for a campus aimed at cloud and AI customers.

The buildings, TYO1 and TYO2, are in Goodman Business Park in Inzai City and will provide a combined 70.8 megawatts of IT capacity. TYO1 is already operating. TYO2 is being developed for more demanding AI computing workloads, with space for liquid cooling to be installed in the future.

The loan carries environmental requirements for the buildings. They must attain an agreed green building certification and meet a design target for energy efficiency. That target is a power usage effectiveness (PUE) ratio of 1.3 or below, meaning the facilities are designed to use no more than 1.3 units of energy for every unit used by their computing equipment.

According to STTGDC, TYO1 has achieved LEED Gold certification and is designed for an annualised ratio below 1.25. Its cooling system is designed to use no additional water during normal operations. TYO2 is also targeting LEED Gold certification.

Standard Chartered led coordination of the financing alongside Mizuho Bank, OCBC, Société Générale and UOB. Standard Chartered and Société Générale were the green loan coordinators.

title: Mercedes joins BMW, VW with outlook cut after China slump
article:
(Oct 27): Mercedes-Benz Group AG cut its profit guidance, joining peers Volkswagen AG and BMW AG after sales in China declined.

The luxury-car maker now sees an adjusted return on sales in its core cars division of between 2% and 3% for the year, it said Tuesday (Oct 27), compared with as high as 5% previously.

Mercedes cited the increasingly tough environment in China as well as higher costs during the fourth quarter, partly driven by higher expenses on materials. The company now expects group earnings before interest and tax to be roughly flat from a year earlier, downgrading its previous forecast for a significant increase.

The shares declined as much as 5.4% following the news, the steepest drop in just over a month. The stock is down by more than a third this year.

The downgrade underscores how quickly China has gone from a dependable profit engine for German automakers to one of their biggest strategic headaches. Falling earnings are leaving them with less room to manoeuvre, just as they need to spend heavily to reposition their businesses.

The cut will also intensify scrutiny of CEO Ola Källenius’s strategy of concentrating on higher-priced cars. Mercedes now has to protect the brand in China while financing a heavy product rollout and restructuring a German cost base built for stronger volumes.

See also: Porsche profit holds firm as 911 cushions sales slump

title: Spain eases data centre energy rules in win for Big Tech
article:
(Oct 27): Spain is easing rules for data center power usage and granting them more time to adapt to the new framework, after an initial government proposal faced strong industry backlash.

The revised draft introduces a transition regime over several years if data centre operators cannot match 80% of their energy consumption with renewable every hour of the day. Instead, under the new terms, projects will have to meet 60% of their electricity demand with renewable energy during peak hours, known as P1, until 2029, according to a copy of the draft seen by Bloomberg.

That requirement will climb to 70% in 2029, and then to 80% in 2032. The original tougher proposal would have introduced an 80% level all day immediately.

Spain has become one of Europe’s biggest markets for data centres, largely due to its cheap energy, with the likes of Amazon.com Inc, Microsoft Corp, Blackstone Inc and Merlin Properties Socimi SA all investing in the country. Industry group SpainDC expects IT capacity to rise nearly sixfold to 2.5GW from 2025 to 2030.

The trend faces opposition from the government, which says data centres could push electricity prices up for other consumers and add little value to the broader economy. Earlier this month, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said that they are an “extractive” business and officials have repeatedly criticised the facilities as financial deals rather than industrial projects.

The government first unveiled the plans in late August, heightening the tensions with industry.

See also: Sembcorp explores supplying low-carbon power to Singtel’s Nxera

Under the revised rules, data centres will also be required to increase the amount of renewable energy to 60% during the second-highest-demand periods, known as P2. This requirement will start in 2029.

The amended draft also relaxes a requirement that renewable power come from newly built power sites. They will be allowed to be 36 months old, compared with the previous proposal of 16 months. Solar plants will be removed from this requirement.

The government says the new rules will prioritise projects that are most likely to be built while discouraging companies from hoarding scarce grid capacity.

See also: Data centres get a reality check

The new proposal was sent to a key government consulting body Monday.

title: Vivian Balakrishnan visits Indonesia after natural gas cuts
article:
(Oct 27): Singapore Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan is scheduled to meet his Indonesian counterpart in Jakarta on Tuesday, days after Indonesia trimmed natural gas exports to the city-state.

A meeting with Indonesia’s Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir is scheduled for 3pm Jakarta Time, according to the country’s foreign ministry, which added that a joint statement is expected after the meeting.

Singapore’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the meeting.

Relations between the two countries have recently been rattled by Jakarta’s unexpected decision to trim natural gas supplies to the city-state.

Indonesian Energy and Mineral Resources Minister Bahlil Lahadalia said Monday that the cuts weren’t deep enough to constitute a breach of commercial contracts. Singapore’s Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry has said it’s checking with buyers to confirm that, but said Tuesday that it welcomes the “clarification” from Indonesia that its suppliers will honour their contracts.

That move had followed simmering tensions over the regional impact of haze from fires across Indonesia. President Prabowo Subianto and some members of its government directed angst toward unnamed neighbouring countries. Singapore is looking into 10 locally registered firms with Indonesia land operations.

See also: Singapore must work faster to vie with wealth hubs, says deputy PM

Separately, former Indonesian trade minister Muhammad Lutfi accused Singapore’s Temasek Holdings Pte Ltd and GIC Pte Ltd of pressuring MSCI Inc to consider downgrading the country’s stocks. Both state-owned funds denied the accusations.

title: Porsche profit holds firm as 911 cushions sales slump
article:
(Oct 27): Porsche AG’s profitability held up despite another sharp decline in vehicle sales, as demand for 911 sports cars and high-priced derivatives helped cushion the slump in China and weaker factory utilisation.

The automotive division posted a 6.9% operating margin for the first nine months, compared with 0.2% a year ago, while group operating profit recovered to €1.74 billion from €0.04 billion a year earlier. Revenue was €25.3 billion, versus €26.9 billion a year earlier.

Porsche retained its full-year forecasts for revenue of €35 billion to €36 billion and a group operating margin of 5.5% to 7.5%. Maintaining the outlook signals confidence in the fourth quarter, with analysts’ revenue estimates currently sitting just above the bottom of the range.

CEO Michael Leiters is working to repair a profit formula built on strong Chinese demand, high factory utilisation and a steady flow of lucrative new models. All three have weakened at once while US tariffs and Porsche’s costly reversals on electric vehicles have left the company, majority owned by Volkswagen AG, spending heavily just as its former growth engine contracts.

The 911 remains Porsche’s strongest defence. Deliveries of the sports car rose even as the wider business shrank, and buyers continued to favour expensive GTS, Turbo and GT versions. That mix is helping offset China and gaps left by the combustion-engine Macan and 718, but it cannot fully compensate for plants and development operations designed for much higher volumes.

Leiters’s first task is to shrink Porsche for a tougher era. The company plans to eliminate more than 9,000 positions, cut management ranks by 40% and lower the annual volume needed to break even to about 200,000 vehicles. He is also reducing development spending and concentrating resources on fewer, more profitable projects.

See also: Audi splits logos for China as carmaker fights to revive sales

Only then does Porsche intend to push decisively further upmarket. The strategy includes increasing prices of its most exclusive sports cars by about 20%, expanding bespoke and track-focused offerings and introducing models above the 911. The quarter offers early evidence of whether Porsche can preserve enough profit and cash during the cost-cutting phase to finance that more ambitious second act.

title: Orange boosts profit outlook after Africa, Middle East growth
article:
(Oct 27): Orange SA raised its profit outlook for the third time this year, driven by growth across all the French mobile carrier’s markets.

Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation after leases will grow more than 4.5% for the full year, the Paris-based telecommunications company said in a statement on Tuesday. That’s up from a previous forecast of more than 4%.

Third-quarter Ebitdaal rose to €4.14 billion (US$4.6 billion), Orange said, slightly above analysts’ average estimate of €4.09 billion, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

The bulk of Orange’s growth for the period came from its Africa and Middle East markets, both increasingly important engines for the company as competition weighs on its more mature European businesses. It offers mobile, broadband and financial services in the region.

In Europe, the French telecom operator has been seeking greater scale through consolidation. Orange joined rivals Bouygues Telecom and Iliad SA in a €20.4 billion deal to acquire billionaire Patrick Drahi’s SFR in France. If approved by regulators, the transaction would reduce the French market from four major operators to three, potentially easing intense price competition. Orange said it expects the deal to close in the second half of next year, and that negotiations with SFR’s employee works council over the sale process were ongoing.

Earlier this year, Orange also acquired the remaining stake in its MasOrange joint venture in Spain from private equity investors.

See also: Japan vows to address cyber attack on FX with urgency

Like other telecommunications companies in Europe, Orange is trying to evolve beyond its core business, exploring data centres and satellites as potential areas for growth.

Orange partnered with infrastructure manager Morrison in July for a French data-centre venture and is part of a consortium bidding for an EU-subsidised data centre project in France.

It also joined a group effort with Deutsche Telekom AG, Vodafone Group Plc and Telefonica SA to bid for satellite spectrum in Europe to fend off potential competition from SpaceX’s Starlink as the latter expands into mobile connectivity.

title: Meta upsizes equity offering as it seeks almost US$98 bil
article:
(Oct 27): Meta Platforms Inc is seeking to raise as much as US$97.5 billion from selling common and preferred stock, supporting its development in artificial intelligence with one of the largest equity offerings in history.

The company sold US$12.5 billion of preferred shares at US$50 apiece and US$25 billion of common stock at US$625 per share, according to a statement late on Monday. The common stock offering was upsized from US$22.5 billion. Meta also plans to raise as much as about US$60 billion in an at-the-market share sale programme, which allows companies to sell shares in the open market from time to time. The ATM will consist of its planned Class C nonvoting shares.

Nvidia Corp, Advanced Micro Devices Inc and Broadcom Inc agreed to buy as much as US$5 billion of the common shares in aggregate, the company said earlier. Meta intends to use the proceeds to support its investment in AI infrastructure and personal superintelligence.

Meta’s shares slipped 1.7% to US$631.51 at 9.53am in New York. Its shares have fallen 2.7% this year through Friday’s close.

Earlier this year, Alphabet Inc and Intel Corp also held rare stock sales in order to support investment in AI initiatives, which require massive amounts of infrastructure and computing power. Both sales were oversubscribed.

Meta’s CEO Mark Zuckerberg overhauled the company’s AI operation through an aggressive hiring push and has launched new products as well as committed hundreds of billions of dollars to build out the infrastructure needed to support the models. The company also has unveiled a personal AI agent known as Muse and an AI model called Muse Wonder, which leadership says is on par with OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic PBC’s Claude in terms of tasks such as coding.

See also: OCBC draws AI ideas from staff beyond tech teams as it builds skills across the bank

The first part of the offering consisted of 250 million depositary shares that represent a 1/20th interest in mandatory convertible preferred shares. Details of the ATM programme have yet to be determined, the statement shows.

Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs Group Inc are leading Meta’s share offerings, according to the statement.

During its earnings report, Meta announced a new class of nonvoting stock that could ultimately be used to help pay for acquisitions and other expenses. Meta’s Class C shares will be distributed to existing investors through a stock dividend. Holders will get one share of the new stock in what will essentially be a two-for-one stock split, Meta said. It expects trading of the new shares to begin in January.

title: Oil declines as Iran diplomacy picks up before Israeli, US votes
article:
(Oct 27): Oil fell further from a six-month high on hopes diplomacy may avert a flareup in the US-Iran war, with elections looming, including in Israel.

Brent dropped below US$115 a barrel after losing almost 1% in the previous session, while West Texas Intermediate was near US$101. Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey travelled to Tehran for discussions on Monday, with participants agreeing to more talks, IRIB news agency reported.

Elsewhere, Russian President Vladimir Putin is due to meet on Tuesday with his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian, as well as Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, on the sidelines of an energy summit in Moscow. Russia has been a key ally for Tehran during the months-long conflict.

Still, risks remain acute even as crude flows have recovered to around prewar levels, while shipping costs are elevated. In Lebanon, Hezbollah is preparing for a new war after receiving funds from Iran, Reuters said. A Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed four drones targeting the kingdom’s south, and three ballistic missiles aimed at the east, launched by Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

“The market is balancing the bearish signals of a restoration of oil flow from the Middle East and reports of diplomatic Iranian channels remaining open,” said Saul Kavonic, senior energy analyst at MST Marquee. Prices could move substantially either way, depending on whether the conflict escalates, he said.

Global benchmark Brent has surged by almost 90% this year, as the US-Iran war disrupted energy flows and drew Yemen’s Houthi rebels into the conflict, with attacks on Saudi Arabia. Investors are bracing for a packed stretch of potential market catalysts, with Israeli elections on Tuesday, a Federal Reserve (Fed) decision later this week, and the US midterms on Nov 3.

See also: Woodside sells stake in long-stalled Timor-Leste LNG project

In the Israeli contest, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pledging to topple Tehran’s regime, with US President Donald Trump’s backing. His challenger, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, says Iran’s nuclear programme must be stopped, but he’s added that regime change is “not an achievable goal”.

The US midterms offer another potential inflection point, as Trump has suggested that strikes against Iran could resume following the vote. At the weekend, the president told Fox News it was “getting to be decision time” on whether to reach a deal with Tehran or “finish it off”.

For now, Washington’s forces are blockading Iran’s ports to choke off the Islamic Republic’s crude shipments, while assisting flows through the Strait of Hormuz from other Persian Gulf producers. In Monday’s talks, Iran informed Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan that it’s flexible on a proposal to reopen the waterway in exchange for the lifting of the US curbs in seven days.

See also: European gas hits €97 for first time since 2022 on winter risks
• Brent for December settlement dropped 1% to US$114.63 a barrel at 1.09pm in Singapore.

Despite the fall in futures, Brent’s prompt spread — the difference between its two closest contracts — remains in steep backwardation, a bullish pattern. On Monday, the gap was near US$5 a barrel, up from US$3.69 a week ago.

“Considering the limited odds of the US striking Iran before the midterm elections on Nov 3, versus a much greater chance after the elections, I find it rather odd that the backwardation continues to expand,” said Robert Yawger, director of the energy futures division at Mizuho Securities USA LLC, highlighting the expiry of the December contract at the end of the week.

The Fed will deliver its policy decision on Wednesday, after tightening last month for the first time since 2023 to tackle still-too-hot inflation. In the run-up, Fed officials suggested they were in no hurry to raise interest rates again, despite gains in energy costs such as diesel.

title: Dubai firm’s US$543 mil IPO covered within minutes despite war
article:
(Oct 27): DIP Holding plc drew enough demand to cover its up to US$543 million initial public offering within minutes of opening books, signalling strong appetite for the United Arab Emirates’ first listing since the Iran war began.

Dubai Investments PJSC is offering a 20% stake in DIP at 1.10 dirhams to 1.15 dirhams apiece. At the top of the range, DIP Holding would be valued at 10 billion dirhams. Indicated demand for the offer exceeds the number of shares on offer, according to terms seen by Bloomberg News.

The company is offering investors US$592 million in dividend payouts over the next three years. Based on the expected annual payout of 725 million dirhams for 2027, the price range implies a yield of as much as 7.60%.

Some investors had called for DIP to temper its valuation expectations and offer higher payouts, closer to the roughly 9% yield from developer Emaar Properties PJSC, given geopolitical concerns, Bloomberg News has reported.

The deal comes as the Iran war amplifies a slowdown in Gulf IPO markets. Regional stocks have also come under pressure since the conflict began in late February, with Dubai’s exchange down around 5% this year.

While the IPO market has been slow, deal activity in the Middle East has continued despite the regional conflict. In just the past 24 hours, Apollo Global Management Inc. bought a stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset management arm of Abu Dhabi’s US$385 billion sovereign wealth fund, while Investcorp teamed up with Saudi investors to buy a fire safety and equipment company, one of the first inbound deals in the kingdom since the war with the Iran-backed Houthis escalated.

See also: Anthropic flags ‘existential risks’ in long-awaited IPO filing

DIP Holding owns Dubai Investments Park, a 2,300-hectare (8.9 square mile) development located close to two of Dubai’s major logistics hubs: Jebel Ali Port, which has been severely disrupted by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and Al Maktoum International Airport, which is undergoing a US$35 billion expansion. Among the largest mixed-use projects in the UAE, it houses warehouses, hotels, retailers, schools and healthcare facilities.

Dubai Investments’ wider portfolio includes holdings in roughly 30 businesses across industries including manufacturing, property and financial services. It has previously also earmarked Emirates Glass LLC and district-cooling company Emicool LLC as listing candidates.

The subscription period for the DIP offering will run from Oct 27 to Nov 3, and shares are expected to begin trading on Dubai’s bourse on Nov 11.

title: Jio shares indicated 22% higher in India grey-market trading
article:
(Oct 27): For investors lucky enough to land shares in Jio Platforms Ltd’s US$3.1 billion India-record initial public offering, trading on the unofficial market is fuelling hopes of a big debut pop.

Billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s digital and telecommunications giant has attracted stellar demand across investor categories ahead of its Oct 28 market debut. Investors who got their allocations on Tuesday are now closely watching Jio’s grey-market pricing for clues about how the first day might unfold. The premium over the IPO price has hovered at about 22% for roughly 10 days, unusually resilient for an offering of this size, according to the ipowatch.in and investorgain.com platforms.

Grey market premiums are unregulated and provide no guarantee of where a stock will actually trade once it hits the exchange. Still, they are widely tracked in India as a barometer of demand and listing-day sentiment.

If the pattern holds in the listing, it would make Jio India’s second-most valuable company after parent Reliance Industries Ltd, pushing rival Bharti Airtel Ltd into third place. That prospect is adding to the excitement around an IPO that’s already rewritten records in India’s capital markets. Jio attracted more than US$78 billion in bids and nearly 14 million applications in one of the country’s most anticipated listings.

So far, Jio has been able to defy the usual trend of grey market premiums cooling after an IPO closes, as the initial rush of bidding fades and investors shift their focus to allotments and the eventual listing. After National Stock Exchange of India Ltd's US$2.4 billion IPO, the premium gradually eroded from about 15% to 3% in two weeks and the shares ultimately made a relatively muted debut.

See also: Jio’s record India IPO falls short of record payday for bankers

The optimism is backed by blockbuster subscription numbers. Jio’s IPO was subscribed more than 22 times, with qualified institutional buyers bidding for 71 times the shares reserved for them. Wealthy investors subscribed 14 times their allocation while the retail portion was covered 2.7 times. The offering was fully subscribed within just 100 minutes of opening last week, even as a bruising selloff swept through Indian equities.

title: China’s 5-year government bond yield trades near record low
article:
(Oct 27): China’s five-year government bond yield dropped after the central bank increased its cash injection into the banking system.

The yield on five-year sovereign notes briefly touched 1.34% to head for the lowest closing level on record, based on Chinabond data going back to 2002. It had also briefly declined below the record close on an intraday basis last week.

The People’s Bank of China earlier injected a net RMB1.01 trillion via reverse repurchases in open market operations, the highest daily net injection on record, Bloomberg data show.

title: China property woes bring strains to Huafa’s US$62 bil of debt
article:
(Oct 27): China’s unprecedented property crisis has just reached another flashpoint, as one of the country’s biggest local-government-owned conglomerates struggles with debt payments.

Based in the southern province of Guangdong, Zhuhai Huafa Group Co missed payments on two trust products that were due recently, people familiar with the matter said on Monday. The firm, which has helped build landmarks such as the 330m tall Zhuhai Tower skyscraper, has also been asking to extend loans from at least three banks.

That makes it the largest company heavily reliant on the property sector to try pushing back debt payments since China Vanke Co, once the country’s biggest developer, took similar steps about a year ago.

The development underscores how China’s years-long real estate debt woes are still spreading despite recent signs of stabilisation in the housing market. Huafa has developed over 200 residential projects across China. The conglomerate had RMB413 billion of interest-bearing liabilities, including bank and trust loans as well as bonds, as of March, according to a company document this month.

“Huafa is facing the same challenges as other Chinese developers but it also plays such a crucial role in the local economy that local governments are highly likely to step in and support it,” said Yao Yu, CEO and founder of credit research firm RatingDog. “The eventual repayment outlook of Huafa’s bonds is not overly pessimistic.”

See also: Seven adjoining Hillview Terrace factories launched for sale at $51.6 mil

Still, the news this week sparked sharp declines in bonds and shares tied to the group, which had just priced a RMB1 billion note in the domestic market at the relatively low cost of 2.07% only a few days ago.

One of Huafa’s offshore yuan-denominated bonds was last indicated down by a record 17% Tuesday, bringing it to about 74% of face value.

Shares of Zhuhai Huafa Properties Co, the real estate arm of Huafa Group, fell as much as 8.9% in Shanghai Tuesday, to the lowest intra-day level in more than a month.

See also: One Comcentre earns ‘industry-leading’ customer experience rating

Unlike Vanke, which is only partially backed by a state-owned firm in Shenzhen, Huafa is wholly owned by the Guangdong government, with Zhuhai’s State-Owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission holding about 93.5% and the provincial finance department owning the remainder.

Local rating firm China Lianhe Credit Rating affirmed Huafa’s AAA rating earlier this year, despite its heavy debt burden, weakening profitability and its high reliance on external financing. The credit assessor cited expectations of strong local government support, given Huafa’s status as a major conglomerate owned by Zhuhai.

After a downward spiral for five years, China’s home prices fell at a slower pace last month, fuelling hopes that the property market is turning a corner. China’s government recently turned to mortgage subsidies and changes to bank lending policies to step up efforts to support the economy.

Huafa, which derived about half of its revenue from property development and urban operations last year while also running businesses spanning financial services and technology, had blamed the property downturn as the main reason for its profitability swings.

It reported a total loss of RMB16.9 billion last year and had about RMB765 billion in total assets as of March.

“Local government-backed Chinese developers are likely to remain under pressure amid weak homebuyer sentiment, falling property sales and limited fiscal capacity at many regional governments,” said Andrew Chan, credit analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence. “Unlike centrally backed SOEs, they face weaker funding access and refinancing support.”

title: Chinese firm’s investor dispute shows dark side of HK listings
article:
(Oct 27): A dispute involving a Chinese technology firm at the centre of a deal-rigging probe is pulling back the curtain on the sometimes murky details of dealmaking around Hong Kong initial public offerings, just as regulators mount a historic crackdown on suspected market distortions.

The fallout at Tianju Dihe Suzhou Technology Co underscores concerns raised by the city’s securities watchdog. The company is under scrutiny for suspected IPO rigging, its shares have been suspended and senior executives have resigned after a deal linked to a cornerstone backer soured. Both the company and the investor are in the crosshairs of an investigation looking into suspected schemes to create false demand. One of the key red flags the regulator has advised market participants to be vigilant about is listing companies making substantial investments or loans to prospective investors.

At the centre of the episode is a series of transactions around Tianju Dihe’s 2024 IPO. A forensic probe, commissioned by the company after audit questions emerged, found that the data processor invested with two firms after limited vetting. When the notes allegedly matured at dates Tianju Dihe thought had been agreed on, the money never returned. It’s unclear whether the regulatory action was triggered by the probe or started independently of it.

The Suzhou-based company invested in US$6 million worth of so-called cash-management notes with Reynold Lemkins Group Asia Ltd — a cornerstone investor in its IPO — and another US$4 million with Kaufmann & Company Pan-Asia Ltd, a company Tianju Dihe later said had been in a business relationship with Reynold Lemkins. Tianju Dihe is now pursuing legal action in a dispute over the notes, alleging that Reynold Lemkins and Kaufmann didn’t make repayments or distributions.

Tianju Dihe and Yang Dong, a person tied to Kaufmann, didn’t respond to requests for comment. A query sent to an email address listed on Reynold Lemkins’ website couldn’t be delivered.

Hong Kong regulators recently highlighted concerns about the overreliance on IPO-related networks and intermediaries as they stepped up the scrutiny of the city’s booming market for listings. Tianju Dihe’s disclosure offers a rare glimpse into the inner workings of relationships forged during a deal process and how they can evolve into subsequent investment transactions.

See also: Chinese PCB maker Dongshan raises US$1.3 bil in HK listing

The Securities and Futures Commission this month announced one of the most sweeping enforcement actions in Hong Kong’s history. The regulator suspended bubble tea maker Sichuan Baicha Baidao Industrial Co’s stock as it investigates a suspected case of IPO rigging, while it also issued restriction notices to 31 brokers, prohibiting them from dealing with or processing assets relating to two syndicates on three listings.

Separately, the SFC said it had identified cases in which listing applicants may have entered into undisclosed arrangements with investors, without specifying the deals. It pinpointed payments made by listing candidates — loans or investments in favour of investors — among red flags that can help market participants identify “dubious arrangements”.

As part of the measures, the watchdog also restricted 29 brokers from dealing with assets of up to HK$285 million in client accounts related to Tianju Dihe’s IPO.

See also: Hong Kong IPO red flags include sudden loans and secret handshakes

The company detailed its findings before the SFC this month said it was taking action against Tianju Dihe, Reynold Lemkins, Kaufmann and Liu Haoran, an individual, for suspected fraud to create the false or artificial appearance of IPO demand.

Tianju Dihe, whose stock has been suspended since April 2025, made the disclosures after the stock exchange ordered an independent investigation into audit issues. The probe found the company had not verified Reynold Lemkins and Kaufmann’s licences or qualifications, and that the firm had relied on due-diligence work conducted by professional parties rather than conducting its own vetting.

The company was introduced to Reynold Lemkins for a potential cornerstone investment by its then-sole sponsor of the deal, it said, citing the investigator’s finding. Listing documents now show Citic Securities Co as the IPO’s sole sponsor.

Tianju Dihe had said its subscription of Reynold Lemkins notes wasn’t an indirect benefit or side arrangement given for being a cornerstone investor.

As a form of remedy, the company’s founder Zuo Lei agreed to take up all US$10 million of the notes. Zuo, who was chairman and chief executive officer, and two executives resigned in August as a result of the need for “improvement in the company’s internal control system and a need to implement additional internal control procedures", the company said in a filing.
